g10-chemistry-uc5-t1.overview: Metals built civilisation — from bronze tools to the iron industry to the aluminium in modern aircraft. This lesson covers why metals behave the way they do (their bonding), how their position in the reactivity series dictates extraction chemistry, and how ores become pure metal in furnaces from a blast furnace to electrolysis.
objectives: Relate metallic bonding to physical properties (conductivity, malleability, luster)
Compare chemical properties of metals (reaction with O₂, water, acids)
Use the reactivity series to predict extraction methods
Describe blast-furnace iron extraction with equations
Explain electrolytic extraction of aluminium and reasons for each step
g10-chemistry-uc5-t1.simple: Metals are bundles of positive ions swimming in a sea of delocalised electrons — that electron glue explains everything: electricity flows because the electrons move, wires bend because ion layers slide without snapping, shine comes from electrons reflecting light. Chemically, metals lose electrons (they're reducing agents), and the reactivity series ranks how eagerly: K Na Ca Mg Al Zn Fe ... Cu Ag Au. How you DIG a metal out of its ore depends on that rank: unreactive metals (Au) sit in nature already pure; medium ones (Fe, Zn) get reduced with carbon in a furnace; reactive ones (Al, Na) need electricity (electrolysis) because carbon can't wrest their oxygen away.
g10-chemistry-uc5-t1.detailed:
Metallic bonding: metal atoms release outer electrons into a shared 'sea' of delocalised electrons holding positive ions together in a giant lattice. Non-directional bonding → ions can slide (malleable/ductile) without fracture; mobile electrons carry charge (conductors) and thermal energy (malleability/heat); electrons interact with light → metallic luster. Melting points vary with charge density: Na (low, 98 °C) vs Fe (1539 °C) vs W (3422 °C — filament metal).

Physical property summary: high density, high melting/boiling points (mostly), solids at room temp (except Hg), sonorous, good conductors. Exceptions worth naming: Hg liquid, Ga melts in your hand (29.8 °C), alkali metals soft enough to cut with a knife, Os/Ir densest.

Chemical properties: metals + O₂ → basic oxides (2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO); with water: K/Na/Ca cold water → hydroxide + H₂, Mg/Zn steam → oxide + H₂, Cu/Ag nothing; with dilute acids: metal above H → salt + H₂ (Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂); with salt solutions: displacement per the series. Corrosion: rusting needs BOTH oxygen and water; salt accelerates it; prevention = barriers (paint, grease, plating), galvanising (sacrificial Zn), alloying (stainless steel).

Extraction principle: ores are metal compounds (oxides, carbonates, sulfides) — extraction = reduction (remove oxygen / gain electrons). Method by position in series:
• Below H (Au, Ag, Pt): found native; physical separation (panning gold).
• Middle (Zn, Fe, Sn, Pb): reduce oxide with carbon/coke — cheap and effective.
• Above (Al, Mg, Na, K): carbon too weak → electrolysis of molten compound (expensive electricity → expensive metal).

Blast furnace (iron): charge: iron ore (Fe₂O₃) + coke (C) + limestone (CaCO₃) into top; preheated air blast at bottom. Reactions: C + O₂ → CO₂ (exothermic, ~2000 °C); CO₂ + C → 2CO (the reducing agent); Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ (reduction of ore). Limestone decomposes (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂) and CaO + SiO₂ (sand impurity) → CaSiO₃ (slag, floats, tapped off — also prevents iron from absorbing sulfur). Molten iron (pig iron, ~4% C) collects at the bottom. Steelmaking: blow O₂ through pig iron to burn off excess carbon (Fe with 0.2–1.5% C).

Aluminium by electrolysis (Hall–Héroult): Al₂O₃ (from bauxite, purified) dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) — lowers melting point from 2050 °C to ~950 °C, saves enormous energy. Carbon-lined tank = cathode; carbon anodes dipped in. Cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al(l) (sinks to bottom, tapped). Anode: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻; the O₂ burns the carbon anode (C + O₂ → CO₂) so anodes must be replaced. Overall: 2Al₂O₃ → 4Al + 3O₂. Recycling Al uses only ~5% of the electrolysis energy — why recycling matters.

formulas.name: Iron extraction core reactions
formulas.formula: C + O₂ → CO₂ | CO₂ + C → 2CO | Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂
formulas.meaning: Coke makes the reducer (CO); CO reduces the ore.
formulas.example: 160 g Fe₂O₃ (M=160) → 1 mol → 2 mol Fe = 112 g iron.

formulas.name: Aluminium electrolysis
formulas.example: Every 102 g Al₂O₃ yields 54 g Al.

formulas.name: Rust formula (simplified)
formulas.meaning: Iron + oxygen + water → flaky oxide that exposes fresh metal.
formulas.example: Why salt-sprayed coastal gates rust fastest.

workedExamples.problem: Explain, using bonding, why copper conducts electricity but sulfur (S₈) does not.
workedExamples.substitution: Cu: delocalised electrons free to drift under a voltage. S₈: discrete molecules held by weak forces, all electrons locked in covalent bonds — nothing mobile.
workedExamples.answer: Copper's electron sea carries current; molecular sulfur has no free charges — insulator.

workedExamples.problem: Predict and balance: (a) potassium + cold water; (b) zinc + steam; (c) copper + dilute HCl.
workedExamples.substitution: (a) K above all: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂ (violent, lilac flame). (b) Zn middle: Zn + H₂O(g) → ZnO + H₂ (steam only). (c) Cu below H: NO reaction.
workedExamples.answer: K fizzes/explodes, Zn reacts with steam slowly, Cu sits unchanged in acid.

workedExamples.problem: In a blast furnace, 800 g of Fe₂O₃ is fully reduced. What mass of iron forms? (Fe=56, O=16)
workedExamples.answer: 560 g of iron (70% of the ore's mass is metal).

workedExamples.problem: Why is cryolite added when electrolysing alumina, and why must the carbon anodes be continuously replaced?
workedExamples.substitution: Pure Al₂O₃ melts at ~2050 °C (energy madness); in molten cryolite it dissolves and electrolyses at ~950 °C. At the anode, O²⁻ → O₂, and hot carbon reacts: C + O₂ → CO₂.
workedExamples.calculation: The anode literally burns away as CO₂.
workedExamples.answer: Cryolite saves energy; anodes are consumed by the oxygen they produce — replacement is built into the process.

workedExamples.problem: A student says 'aluminium doesn't corrode because it's unreactive.' Correct the statement.
workedExamples.given: Common observation: Al stays shiny outdoors.
workedExamples.substitution: Al IS reactive (above Zn even) — but it reacts instantly with O₂ to form a THIN, STRONG, IMPERMEABLE Al₂O₃ layer that seals the metal beneath.
workedExamples.calculation: Contrast rust: Fe₂O₃·xH₂O is flaky and porous → keeps corroding.
workedExamples.answer: Aluminium is reactive but self-protecting; its oxide skin is the shield (anodising thickens it deliberately).

commonMistakes: Saying metals conduct because atoms 'touch' — it's the DELOCALISED electrons that carry charge.
Claiming all metals are hard/high-melting — Na, K are soft and low-melting; Hg is liquid.
Writing the blast-furnace reducer as carbon instead of carbon MONOXIDE (CO does the Fe₂O₃ reduction).
Thinking slag is unwanted junk only — it also removes sand/sulfur impurities and protects the melt.
Forgetting cryolite's purpose (energy saving) and naming it as 'the electrolyte that provides aluminium'.
Believing aluminium doesn't react — it reacts but passivates with a protective oxide film.
Confusing cathode (reduction, Al forms) and anode (oxidation, O₂ forms) in electrolysis cells.
Saying galvanising 'paints on zinc' — Zn is sacrificial: it corrodes IN PLACE OF iron even when scratched.
applications: Ethiopian context: iron-working traditions (Ethiopian steel 'wook' blades), MESOB steel-rolling ambitions and the Repph Steel plant near Adama.
Aluminium foil & aircraft: light + strong + self-protecting oxide.
Copper wiring & Ethiopian power-grid expansion: conductivity + ductility.
Galvanised roofing sheets (very common in Addis construction): sacrificial zinc protection.
Sodium via electrolysis of molten NaCl (Downs cell) — same series logic as Al.
Recycling metals: Al recycling saves ~95% of primary energy — economic AND environmental.
g10-chemistry-uc5-t1.summary: Metallic bonding (ion + electron sea) → conductivity, malleability, luster. Chemical behaviour = electron donation, ranked by the reactivity series. Extraction follows the series: native (Au) → carbon reduction (Fe blast furnace: C→CO₂→CO, Fe₂O₃+3CO→2Fe+3CO₂, limestone makes slag) → electrolysis for reactive metals (Al₂O₃ in cryolite at 950 °C; anodes burn away). Corrosion is redox; protection = barriers, galvanising, alloying.

steps: Ore: Fe₂O₃ + coke + limestone in top

Why? Because Bonding — tap to reveal

pairs.q: Why does a metal wire bend but table salt shatter?
pairs.a: Ion layers in metal slide through the electron sea; in NaCl, sliding brings like charges together → repulsion cracks the crystal.

pairs.q: Why is rust left unprotected but aluminium shine kept?
pairs.a: Rust (hydrated Fe₂O₃) is flaky and porous — fresh iron keeps attacking. Al₂O₃ is thin, tough and sealed — it stops further attack.

pairs.q: Why replace anodes in aluminium smelting?
pairs.a: The anode carbon reacts with the oxygen made at it (C + O₂ → CO₂) — it literally burns away.

questions.q: Metals conduct electricity because of:
questions.explanation: Mobile delocalised electrons drift under a potential difference.

questions.q: Which metal is extracted by electrolysis rather than carbon reduction?
questions.explanation: Al is too reactive — carbon cannot reduce Al₂O₃; electricity supplies the electrons.

questions.q: Mass of Fe (g) from full reduction of 160 g Fe₂O₃? (Fe₂O₃=160, Fe=56)
questions.explanation: 1 mol Fe₂O₃ → 2 mol Fe = 112 g.

questions.q: The actual reducing agent inside a blast furnace is carbon ____.
questions.explanation: CO₂ + C → 2CO; CO then reduces the iron oxide.

questions.q: Why is limestone added to the blast furnace?
questions.answer: removes impurities slag|forms calcium silicate|removes sand silica
questions.explanation: CaCO₃ → CaO; CaO + SiO₂ → CaSiO₃ slag, which floats and is tapped off.

questions.q: Cryolite in aluminium electrolysis serves to:
questions.explanation: It dissolves Al₂O₃ so electrolysis runs at ~950 °C instead of ~2050 °C.

questions.q: Mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature.
questions.explanation: The classic exception — Hg melts at −39 °C.

questions.q: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. Moles of H₂ from 0.5 mol Zn (excess acid)?
questions.explanation: 1:1 ratio → 0.5 mol H₂.

questions.q: How does galvanising protect scratched steel?
questions.answer: sacrificial zinc|zinc corrodes instead|zinc more reactive
questions.explanation: Zn is above Fe in the series — it oxidises preferentially, feeding electrons to the iron even at a scratch.

questions.q: Pick the correct reaction sequence for CO formation in the blast furnace:
options: CO₂ + C → 2CO then C + O₂ → CO₂
C + O₂ → CO₂ then CO₂ + C → 2CO
Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe then C + O₂ → CO
CaCO₃ → CaO then C + O₂ → CO₂
questions.explanation: Coke burns first (heat), then hot coke reduces the CO₂ up the stack to CO — the ore reducer.

g10-chemistry-uc5-t2.overview: Oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, chlorine, sulfur and carbon — the non-metals that run industry, medicine and life itself. Learn how each is produced (from lab test-tube to industrial tower), how you prove which gas is in the tube, and where Ethiopia's own resources (Sulphur Springs, the Afar potash and salt works) fit in.
objectives: Describe lab and industrial preparation of O₂, H₂, N₂, CO₂ and chlorine
Perform/interpret the classic gas tests (pop, relight, limewater, litmus)
Explain the Haber process conditions and their compromises
Relate sulfur extraction (Frasch/contact process) to sulfuric acid manufacture
Identify uses and hazards of each non-metal and its key compounds
g10-chemistry-uc5-t2.simple: Non-metals are made by pulling them out of natural compounds. Oxygen: decompose H₂O₂ with MnO₂ catalyst in the lab, or fractionally distil liquid air industrially. Hydrogen: zinc + dilute acid in the lab; steam + methane industrially. Nitrogen: almost free — 78% of air; obtained by fractional distillation and fixed into fertiliser by the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ at 450 °C, 200 atm, iron catalyst). Chlorine: electrolysis of brine (together with NaOH and H₂ — the chlor-alkali industry). Sulfur: mined from salt domes (Frasch process) or recovered from gas refining, then burned to SO₂ and converted to sulfuric acid — the chemical kings' 'blood'. Each gas has a signature test: H₂ pop, O₂ relights a glowing splint, CO₂ milks limewater, Cl₂ bleaches damp litmus.
g10-chemistry-uc5-t2.detailed:
Oxygen: Lab: 2H₂O₂(aq) →(MnO₂) 2H₂O + O₂↑ — MnO₂ catalyses, collected over water (slightly soluble). Also 2KClO₃ →(MnO₂, Δ) 2KCl + 3O₂. Industrial: fractional distillation of liquefied air (−196 °C: N₂ boils off first, O₂ remains at −183 °C). Medical oxygen for hospitals, oxy-acetylene welding, blast-furnace enrichment.

Hydrogen: Lab: Zn + H₂SO₄(dil) → ZnSO₄ + H₂↑ (granulated zinc, collected over water). Industrial: steam reforming of methane: CH₄ + H₂O(g) →(Ni, 700–1100 °C) CO + 3H₂. Uses: ammonia synthesis, hydrogenation of vegetable oils (margarine), rocket fuel, oxy-hydrogen cutting. Hazards: extremely flammable, explosive with air (the pop test proves it).

Nitrogen & ammonia: N₂ from liquid-air fractionation (inert atmosphere for food packing, liquid N₂ cooling). Fixation: Haber process — N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. Conditions: ~450 °C, 150–250 atm, Fe (promoted) catalyst. The COMPROMISE: low temperature favours yield (exothermic) but is too slow; high pressure favours yield (4 → 2 moles) but costs safety/energy; catalyst speeds both ways without shifting yield. Ammonia → fertilisers (urea, ammonium nitrate), HNO₃, explosives, cleaning agents.

Chlorine: Chlor-alkali electrolysis of concentrated brine (NaCl solution): anode 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; cathode 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻; solution becomes NaOH. Products Cl₂ + NaOH + H₂ are all sold. Uses: water disinfection (Addis Ababa drinking-water treatment), PVC, bleaches (NaClO), solvents. Hazards: toxic green gas, dense, bleaches damp litmus white; historically a WWI weapon — handle only in fume hoods.

Sulfur & sulfuric acid: Sulfur occurs native in volcanic salt domes (Frasch process: superheated water melts it underground, pumped up) and is recovered from crude oil/natural gas (Claus process). Ethiopia: Dallol and Afar sulfur deposits, and the long-operating Sulphur Springs mine near Addis. Contact process: S + O₂ → SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst, 450 °C, 1–2 atm); SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → oleum; oleum + water → H₂SO₄ (never bubble SO₃ straight into water — acid mist forms). H₂SO₄ = 'king of chemicals': fertilisers, batteries, detergents, metallurgy.

Carbon (as CO₂ and beyond): CO₂ lab: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂↑ (effervescence; milks limewater). Industrial: from limestone calcination, fermentation. Dry ice (solid CO₂) for cooling; carbon (coke, charcoal, graphite electrodes, activated carbon filters) as reductant and adsorbent.

keyTerms.def: Liquefy air, boil off N₂ (−196 °C) leaving O₂ (−183 °C).
CH₄ + steam → CO + 3H₂ — industrial hydrogen source.
Brine electrolysis giving Cl₂, NaOH, H₂ together.
Melt underground sulfur with superheated water and pump it up.
S → SO₂ → SO₃ → oleum → H₂SO₄ (V₂O₅ catalyst).
Concentrated H₂SO₄ with dissolved SO₃; diluted to acid.
H₂ pop; O₂ relights; CO₂ milky limewater; Cl₂ bleaches litmus.

formulas.name: Lab oxygen
formulas.meaning: Catalytic decomposition; MnO₂ unchanged and recoverable.
formulas.example: 68 g H₂O₂ (2 mol) → 32 g O₂ (1 mol).

formulas.name: Haber equilibrium
formulas.meaning: Exothermic, fewer gas moles on right → cold+high pressure favour yield.
formulas.when: Fertiliser industry; Le Chatelier (G11 links here).

formulas.name: Contact process chain
formulas.formula: S + O₂ → SO₂; 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃; SO₃ + H₂SO₄ → H₂S₂O₇; +H₂O → 2H₂SO₄
formulas.meaning: Sulfur → sulfuric acid in four steps.
formulas.example: 32 g S can theoretically give 98 g H₂SO₄ (1:3 molar chain).

workedExamples.problem: Describe how you would collect three unlabeled gas jars of O₂, CO₂ and H₂ and identify each with a test.
workedExamples.formula: Solubility/density decide collection; classic tests decide identity.
workedExamples.substitution: All three: over water (CO₂ also by upward displacement of air — denser and slightly soluble). Tests: glowing splint relights → O₂; limewater turns milky → CO₂; lit splint squeaky pop → H₂.
workedExamples.calculation: Collection method follows from solubility and density vs air.
workedExamples.answer: Over water for all; relight = O₂, milkiness = CO₂, pop = H₂.

workedExamples.problem: The Haber process runs at 450 °C although the reaction is exothermic. Explain the compromise.
workedExamples.substitution: Thermodynamics: lower T shifts right (more NH₃). Kinetics: cold = glacially slow (N≡N triple bond hard to break). 450 °C + Fe catalyst = acceptable rate with workable yield; unreacted gases recycled.
workedExamples.calculation: High pressure (200 atm) shifts 4 mol gas → 2 mol, boosting yield.
workedExamples.answer: 450 °C is the engineering compromise: fast enough, rich enough, safe enough — with recycling making up the shortfall.

workedExamples.problem: Chlor-alkali electrolysis of brine: write both electrode reactions and state what remains in solution.
workedExamples.formula: Ion discharge rules (Cl⁻ at anode; water reduced at cathode).
workedExamples.substitution: Anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (green gas, bleaches litmus). Cathode: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻.
workedExamples.calculation: Na⁺ + OH⁻ left → sodium hydroxide solution.
workedExamples.answer: Cl₂ (anode), H₂ (cathode), NaOH(aq) in the tank — three products sold together.

workedExamples.problem: From 64 g of sulfur, what maximum mass of H₂SO₄ can the contact process produce? (S=32, H₂SO₄=98)
workedExamples.answer: 196 g sulfuric acid (theoretical maximum; real plants lose a few %).

workedExamples.problem: Why must SO₃ be absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ rather than added directly to water in the contact process?
workedExamples.substitution: SO₃ + H₂O is violently exothermic → creates a fine mist of H₂SO₄ droplets that won't settle or react cleanly.
workedExamples.calculation: Absorbing into acid gives oleum (H₂S₂O₇), then controlled dilution.
workedExamples.answer: Direct water addition makes unmanageable acid mist; oleum lets the plant control the dilution safely.

commonMistakes: Gas test mix-ups: 'pop' is hydrogen, 'relights' is oxygen — swapping them fails every practical exam.
Saying MnO₂ 'reacts away' in H₂O₂ decomposition — it's a catalyst: unchanged, recoverable.
Collecting H₂ by downward displacement of air — it's the LIGHTEST gas: use upward displacement or over water.
Thinking the Haber catalyst increases yield — catalysts speed BOTH directions; only T and P shift equilibrium.
Naming chlorine's litmus effect as 'turns red' — it BLEACHES damp blue litmus white (acid + oxidation).
Writing the Frasch process as mining with picks — it's superheated WATER melting sulfur underground.
Adding water to acid when diluting H₂SO₄ — always ACID into water (heat control), never the reverse.
Confusing oleum with sulfur trioxide — oleum is H₂SO₄ with SO₃ already dissolved in it.
applications: Ethiopian links: Sulphur Springs (Addis) and Dallol/Afar deposits; sugar factories use lime for juice clarification (CO₂ from kilns).
Water treatment: chlorine disinfection of municipal supplies; activated-carbon filters.
Agriculture: NPS/ZGS blended fertilisers from H₂SO₄ + phosphate rock — backbone of Ethiopian cereal yields.
Medical: oxygen therapy; H₂O₂ antiseptic; liquid nitrogen for biological samples.
Food industry: N₂ blanket packaging keeps injera and snacks fresh without oxidation.
g10-chemistry-uc5-t2.summary: O₂: H₂O₂+MnO₂ (lab) / liquid-air distillation (industry). H₂: Zn+acid / steam reforming of CH₄. N₂: air distillation; fixed via Haber (450 °C, 200 atm, Fe — the yield/rate compromise). Cl₂: chlor-alkali brine electrolysis (Cl₂ + NaOH + H₂). S: Frasch/Claus → contact process → H₂SO₄ via oleum. Tests: pop-H₂, relight-O₂, milky-CO₂, bleach-Cl₂.

pairs.q: Why is air the cheapest nitrogen source?
pairs.a: Air is 78% N₂ — liquefy and distil; nothing to mine or react.

pairs.q: Why recycle gases in the Haber process?
pairs.a: Only ~15% converts per pass; unreacted N₂/H₂ are separated and sent back — near-total utilisation.

pairs.q: Why is H₂SO₄ called the king of chemicals?
pairs.a: More tons produced worldwide than any other compound — fertilisers, batteries, dyes, metals all need it.

questions.q: A glowing splint RELIGHTS in a jar. The gas is:
questions.explanation: Oxygen supports combustion — the classic relight test.

questions.q: The catalyst used in H₂O₂ lab oxygen preparation is ____ dioxide.
questions.explanation: MnO₂ speeds decomposition and is unchanged.

questions.q: Industrial hydrogen is mainly made by:
questions.explanation: CH₄ + H₂O(g) → CO + 3H₂ (Ni catalyst) — cheap bulk route.

questions.q: Haber: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Moles of NH₃ from 2 mol N₂ (excess H₂)?
questions.explanation: 1:2 ratio → 4 mol NH₃.

questions.q: Why does the Haber process use high PRESSURE?
questions.answer: fewer moles right|shifts equilibrium to ammonia|4 mol gas become 2
questions.explanation: Left has 4 gas moles, right 2 — pressure favours the side with fewer molecules (more NH₃).

questions.q: Chlorine is produced industrially by:
questions.explanation: Chlor-alkali electrolysis: Cl⁻ oxidised at the anode.

questions.q: Damp blue litmus bleached white indicates chlorine gas.
questions.explanation: Cl₂ + water makes HClO — a strong oxidising bleach.

questions.q: The catalyst in the contact process (SO₂ → SO₃) is vanadium(__) oxide.
questions.explanation: V₂O₅ at ~450 °C.

questions.q: Mass of H₂SO₄ (g) from 32 g sulfur (1:1 chain)? (S=32, H₂SO₄=98)
questions.explanation: 1 mol S → 1 mol H₂SO₄ = 98 g.

questions.q: Choose the correct contact-process order:
questions.explanation: Burn sulfur, catalyse to SO₃, absorb in acid (oleum), then dilute.
